newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Strikes not seen hurting Israel privatisation.
newsitem.headline: Strikes not seen hurting Israel privatisation.

text.p: Strikes by Israeli unions will not threaten the country's privatisation programme, analysts predicted on Thursday following a walkout by some 60,000 telecoms workers.
The Histadrut labour federation launched an open-ended wildcat strike on Thursday in support of communications workers battling the privatisation of Bezeq Israel Telecom.
But analysts said such resistance was part of every nation's privatisation process, and would not cast a shadow over what was left of Israel's privatisation programme.
"One proof of privatisation is when there is a struggle with workers," said Eli Nahum, head of trading at Tel Aviv-based Zannex Securities.
"If the government is confronting employees, it just shows its decisiveness with regard to privatisation."

A spokesman for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called the strike 'unnecessary', adding it would not affect the government's intention of opening the economy to competition while protecting workers' rights.

The stoppage was declared just hours after the government issued an order obliging employees to restore essential telephone services disrupted in a week-long strike at Bezeq, the country's main telecoms provider.
Union leaders said government plans to privatise more of the company through the $250 million sale of 12.5 percent of its stock via US investment bank Merrill Lynch would worsen the crisis.
They said that deal violated government promises to involve Bezeq workers in all aspects of the privatisation, and called for the sale to be cancelled.
Although the strike action was described by some analysts as 'mild', the conflict is expected to continue.
"The government will not cancel the deal with Merrill Lynch. Even the employees don't believe this will happen," Zannex's Nahum said.
Strikes could delay privatisation in the short term, but the process would continue, he predicted.
Keith Phillips of Societe Generale Strauss Turnbull Securities in London said the market expected industrial unrest.

"If Merrill Lynch agrees to take (Bezeq) shares from the government to try and sell them and then the workers go out on strike it's not a great advert but...I don't think it will put people off from buying or bidding for companies."
The government has already sold tranches of Israel Discount Bank, Bank Leumi and United Mizrahi Bank, and is moving ahead with the sale of a controlling stake in Bank Hapoalim.
Analysts said that the remaining companies that could realistically expect to be privatised -- namely the banks -- should not be hit by workers' strikes.
"The banks are different. They are more forward looking," Phillips said.
Political factors would make other state-owned companies much more diffiuclt to privatise, analysts said.

"When you really look at it, what beyond Bezeq has to be privatised? The defence companies are very political. Israel Electric is very political and the water company won't happen," one industry source said.

The sale of El Al Israel Airlines, burdened by heavy security expenses and a costly prohibition against flying on the Jewish Sabbath, and Zim Israel Navigation, which is jointly owned with the Israel Corp, would also be very problematic, analysts said.
